On New Year's Day, at Bhadkeswar temple in Dwarka—an ancient prosperous city on the Arabian Sea, believed to be Lord Krishna's kingdom capital—I was 21 and yearning. I saw a young woman, likely my age or younger, begging near the temple’s stone steps, her face partly hidden by a sheer green dupatta, with two children clinging to her. Sitting on the edge of the stone wall with my legs over raging waves, I sobbed deeply, feeling my old life drain away. I reflected on my identity collapsing, my true nature dissolving after a single glance, and a spiritual rebirth emerging from my inner turmoil. In an alternate vision, I once lay at her feet; she looked at me with supreme knowledge and no desire. Then, three more children ran down to her, playing fondly; as she raised her arm, a baby appeared nursing beneath her dress. Another world might have called this a death. I bought five bowls of cut green mangoes with chili powder and five coconuts for her family from a street vendor. The sea breeze played with my hair. A small girl, about seven or eight, with grey-blue eyes, sun-kissed caramel skin, and knotted hair, ran toward the sea, met the mother, looked back and waved—she sensed my secret and longing, knowing I was once free. I placed the food on the steps, held the mother’s hand, and prayed for her family—a first for me. Waves crashed fiercely; our feet were wet.
